Considering the relative popularity of Rand Paul amongst young voters I think the Republican Party still has an ability renew itself without too much trouble. Secondly a very important theme for people to vote republican is often nationalism and arguably hatred (against minorities/ anything that isn't 'Murican/ support our troops type). Republicans are extremely pragmatic in retaining political power and play the game much better than Democrats do because of that, with them having given up on fighting gay marriage to a large extent already. The attacks against Obamacare will stop (and in fact are already slowing down strongly) and soon no one will remember the party having flipped its position on it.

I think Republican views (and Democrat views, albeit on a lesser scale) are on the verge of a paradigm shift. Look among republicans and ask them if they approve of gay marriage. Among the older crowd (which makes up most of the Republicans in office), between 22%-30% support it, while a whopping 43%-61% of Republicans between 18 and 50 support it.

http://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2014/03/10/61-of-young-republicans-favor-same-sex-marriage/

Also, Republicans in office are becoming more and more radical Christians, to the point of discriminating against gays in the name of their religion, can be explained by the shrinking number of individuals labeling themselves as Christians. A common response of those who see their viewpoints shrinking in support will often radicalize in their beliefs in a egotistical manner to 'hold down the base'.

I have a feeling that Republicans will shift their focus off of social issues and onto economic ones, adopting a more libertarian approach to politics.

They'll do fine because this is even a question. Hitting on what /u/chronos mentioned you're asking this question under the implication that the two parties are substantively different. So long as people continue to believe this while also holding their political ideologies as something that ought be defended than evolved over time then both parties will be just fine. It's in both of the party's perceived best interest to continue coming up with ultimately irrelevant issues that split people down the line and then making the whole election about that.

Why would I say that? The average congressman is a 58 year old professional politician and a millionaire. By and large, these aren't people that are looking to rock the boat. If one ideology or the other started gaining too much influence it would result in actual change. When the parties are relatively evenly split they can continue to blame the other side for failing to do anything which frees them from any obligations of actually accomplishing anything.

I do believe there are definitely some people who actually believe in an ideology and want to push it forward on both sides of the fence but their voices tend to be squelched. Sanders will be an interesting wildcard since he fits the social agenda of the media, but the media is ultimately owned by corporations. Time Warner owns CNN, Comcast owns NBC, Disney owns ABC, and so on. These are the same companies whose influence Sanders wants to crack down on hard against along with the wealth inequality and other economic issues that could put the futures of these megacorps into an unclear place. If he continues to gain momentum I expect to start seeing ever more pieces like this coming out.

The Republican Party is a very big tent. Carl Rove proved in 2000 and again in 2004 that all politics are local. He crafted unique republican messages literally to the zip code each message was delivered in to. The more money that goes into politics the more refined this targeted advertising will become- perhaps targeted advertising to individual IP and mailing addresses is ahead for the next election with unimaginably complex AIs running the entire show. Ultimately, it doesn't matter how much the brand itself is tarnished among popular opinion. When it comes time to rally enough votes to matter, then the votes will be there.

No, the Republican party has not screwed itself. Not yet, anyway. Partly because the GOP is not homogeneous. If some of the more conservative elements of the GOP are able to win out over the Grahams and McCains, I think they'll be okay.
